title: Reverse Words in a String
corePattern: Two Pointers + String Parsing and Reversal
interviewTips: Ask how to define a word: sequence of non-space chars, and whether to trim leading/trailing spaces and collapse multiple spaces to single space.
Trade-off: split/reversed is shortest to code but uses O(n) extra for tokens; scanning from end avoids split overhead; in-place triple-reverse achieves O(1) extra on mutable strings.
Edge-case tip: test empty string, all spaces, single word, and multiple internal spaces to verify no leading/trailing space in output.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Split and Reverse
approaches.intuition: Words are separated by spaces, so splitting on whitespace automatically removes extra spaces. Once we have clean words, reversing their order and joining with single space gives the answer.
approaches.theory: Use language split that discards empty tokens (Python split(), C++ stringstream >>, Java trim + split on regex). Collect tokens into array, iterate reversed, join with single space. This delegates space handling to library.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single pass to split into words plus pass to join, each char processed constant times where n is string length.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Split stores all words and result string, both proportional to n in worst case.

edgeCases: All spaces like '   ' returns empty string
Single word like 'hello' returns same word
Multiple spaces like 'a good   example' collapsed correctly

approaches.name: Approach 2: Two Pointers Scan From End
approaches.intuition: To get reversed word order without storing all words first, scan from the end. Each time skip spaces, then find the start of the current word, copy it directly to answer.
approaches.theory: Maintain i as end of current word and j to find its start: skip spaces with i, then move j left while non-space. Substring s[j+1..i] is one word. Append to result with single space separator. Move i=j and repeat. Each char visited at most twice.

timeComplexity.explanation: Two pointers i and j only move left, each index visited O(1) times, plus O(n) to build output.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only output string plus few pointers; no token array, but output itself is O(n). O(1) auxiliary.

steps: skip spaces, j finds s[5..8]=good, res='example good'
skip spaces, word s[0..0]=a, res='example good a'

edgeCases: Leading/trailing spaces skipped by first while loop
Single char string works with j+1 indexing
Empty or all-space input returns empty without adding separator

approaches.name: Approach 3: Optimal In-Place Triple Reversal
approaches.intuition: Reversing the whole string puts words in correct reversed order but each word backwards. Reversing each word individually fixes letters, then compact spaces in one pass.
approaches.theory: Step 1 reverse entire char array. Step 2 reverse each maximal non-space block. Step 3 two-pointer compaction: read pointer j scans, write pointer i copies non-space words and inserts single space between them, then resize/truncate. All steps linear and in-place on mutable array.

timeComplexity.explanation: Three linear passes: full reverse, per-word reverse, and compaction. Each char moved O(1) times.

spaceComplexity.explanation: In C++ and Java char array version uses O(1) extra beyond input; Python needs O(n) list because strings immutable, but algorithm itself is O(1) auxiliary.

steps: reverse each word -> 'blue is sky the'
clean spaces -> no change, return 'blue is sky the'

edgeCases: String with only spaces becomes empty after cleanSpaces resize to 0
No extra space at end: only add space if j < n
Single word: double reverse returns original
Already clean input passes through unchanged
